idiom_name: System.Reflection.DispatchProxy.Create<T, TProxy>() + Invoke(MethodInfo, object[]) with a volatile revocation flag
implementation_notes: The forwarder is generated: DispatchProxy.Create<ISession, SessionProxy>() returns an object that implements the interface and routes every method of the generated proxy type to the overridden Invoke(MethodInfo, object[]), which is a single check point for the whole interface. Revocation is a flag that Invoke reads before dispatching - publish it with Volatile (or Interlocked) because otherwise the read can be hoisted and the proxy keeps forwarding - and a hand-written interface wrapper remains the fallback where runtime code generation is not available. .NET adds no revocation of its own, so flag ownership, one-wayness and the failure channel (exception vs Result) are design decisions in the wrapper.
pitfalls: A plain bool written by the revoker and read in Invoke can be cached by the JIT and never observed; the documented atomic primitives (Volatile.Read/Write, Interlocked.Exchange) exist because such read-modify-publish sequences are not atomic by themselves.
The proxy is not the target for identity purposes: reference comparison, dictionary keys and serialisation see the proxy, so code that keys on the target silently stops matching after the grant.
Writing the target into the proxy after Create leaves a window in which a call arriving before wiring dereferences a null target; publish the proxy only after it is fully initialised.
